words.definition: to praise highly, especially in public
words.nuance: Formal; often used for public or official praise.
examples: Critics were quick to laud the director's bold casting choices.
It is easy to laud reform in speeches and much harder to fund it.

words.definition: to praise enthusiastically
words.nuance: Suggests lavish, sometimes excessive praise, often of virtues or benefits.
examples: The brochure goes on to extol the health benefits of cold showers.
Former teachers still extol her as a model student.

words.definition: to praise highly, especially in a speech honoring someone who has died
words.nuance: Comes from the eulogy given at a funeral; also used for glowing tributes to the living.
examples: Colleagues gathered to eulogize the scientist as a generous mentor.
Commentators rushed to eulogize the retiring senator's career.

words.definition: to criticize or reprimand severely
words.nuance: Harsh, often public scolding.
examples: The editorial went on to castigate the council for wasting public funds.
Coaches who castigate players after every mistake rarely build confidence.

words.definition: to express formal, official disapproval of
words.nuance: Usually institutional: a legislature may censure one of its members.
examples: The senate voted to censure the member for misusing campaign funds.
The board chose to censure the firm rather than revoke its license.

words.definition: to speak of as having little value; to belittle
words.nuance: Makes something seem unimportant or inferior, often in a dismissive way.
examples: It is unwise to disparage a rival's work before you have read it.
Some critics disparage genre fiction as mere entertainment.

words.definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action
words.nuance: Implies hardness: unmoved by pleas, argument, or feeling.
examples: Despite the evidence, the manager remained obdurate about the deadline.
Her obdurate refusal to apologize prolonged the feud.

words.definition: unwilling to compromise or change one's views
words.nuance: Common in political and negotiation contexts.
examples: Talks stalled because both sides were intransigent on pay.
An intransigent negotiator can wreck a deal that everyone wants.

words.definition: stubbornly uncooperative toward authority or control
words.nuance: Stresses resistance to being managed or directed.
examples: The recalcitrant mule refused to move another step.
Even the most recalcitrant students warmed to the new teacher.

words.definition: using very few words
words.nuance: Brevity that can seem cool or understated; not necessarily rude.
examples: His laconic reply, a single 'Fine,' told us nothing.
The laconic cowboy is a familiar figure in old westerns.

words.definition: brief and to the point, sometimes to the point of rudeness
words.nuance: Brevity that can come across as curt or unfriendly.
examples: She sent a terse email declining the invitation.
The spokesperson gave a terse statement and left the podium.

words.definition: clearly expressed in few words
words.nuance: Positive: brief and clear, with nothing wasted.
examples: Give me a succinct summary of the findings.
The best abstracts are succinct yet complete.

words.definition: using more words than needed
words.nuance: Describes speech or writing that is padded or wordy.
examples: The verbose report could have been half as long.
Reviewers found the author's style verbose and repetitive.

words.definition: tediously lengthy in speech or writing
words.nuance: Stronger than verbose: the length is boring.
examples: The lecture was so prolix that half the audience drifted off.
Judges grew impatient with the lawyer's prolix arguments.

words.definition: excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
words.nuance: Usually describes a person rather than a piece of writing.
examples: Our garrulous neighbor turned every hello into an hour-long chat.
The garrulous tour guide filled every silence with trivia.

words.definition: showing great care and persistent effort
words.nuance: Emphasizes careful, steady attention to a task.
examples: Thanks to assiduous research, she found the missing letters.
He was assiduous in checking every figure twice.

words.definition: diligent and persevering in attention or effort
words.nuance: A rarer, more formal near-synonym of assiduous.
examples: The archive was assembled through sedulous effort over many years.
A sedulous student, he reviewed his notes every evening.

words.definition: persisting tirelessly
words.nuance: Emphasizes stamina: never seeming to tire.
examples: The indefatigable volunteers worked through the night.
She was an indefatigable advocate for clean water.

words.definition: careful to consider all circumstances and consequences before acting
words.nuance: Suggests looking around carefully before committing.
examples: Investors grew circumspect after the market crash.
Be circumspect about what you post online.

words.definition: feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems
words.nuance: Often implies suspicion of a particular person or thing.
examples: Voters are wary of promises that sound too good to be true.
The cat stayed wary of the new dog for weeks.

words.definition: acting with care and thought for the future
words.nuance: Positive: wise, sensible caution, especially with money or risk.
examples: It would be prudent to save part of every paycheck.
A prudent driver slows down in heavy rain.

words.definition: to drain of energy or vitality
words.nuance: Despite the sound, it means the opposite of 'energize'.
examples: The long, humid afternoon seemed to enervate the whole team.
Years of delay can enervate even the most dedicated reformers.

words.definition: to make very weak and infirm
words.nuance: Often used for illness or severe damage.
examples: A severe flu can debilitate even healthy adults for weeks.
The sanctions were meant to debilitate the regime's war economy.

words.definition: to reduce the force, effect, or value of; to weaken or thin out
words.nuance: Often technical: signals, effects, or concentrations are attenuated.
examples: Thick walls attenuate the noise from the street.
Scientists sought to attenuate the virus so it could be used in a vaccine.

words.definition: calm and peaceful; not easily upset
words.nuance: Used for people, animals, and still water alike.
examples: The placid surface of the lake reflected the mountains.
Even during the crisis, he remained placid and polite.

words.definition: having an unemotional and calm disposition
words.nuance: Can suggest sluggishness or indifference, not only serenity.
examples: The phlegmatic goalkeeper seemed unbothered by the screaming crowd.
Her phlegmatic temperament balanced her anxious partner.

words.definition: unable to be upset or excited; calm
words.nuance: Emphasizes staying calm under pressure.
examples: The imperturbable pilot calmly announced the emergency landing.
She remained imperturbable throughout the hostile interview.

words.definition: not telling the truth; lying
words.nuance: Describes habitual lying or false statements.
examples: The mendacious witness changed his story three times.
Investigators exposed the mendacious claims in the advertisement.

words.definition: deceitful; saying one thing while doing another
words.nuance: Emphasizes double-dealing.
examples: The duplicitous agent was secretly working for both sides.
Voters punished the duplicitous campaign at the polls.

words.definition: not candid or sincere, typically by pretending to know less than one does
words.nuance: A subtle insincerity, often feigned innocence or naivety.
examples: It is disingenuous to claim surprise at a result you predicted.
His apology sounded disingenuous to everyone in the room.

words.definition: extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources
words.nuance: In science, a 'parsimonious' explanation is the simplest one that fits, a positive sense.
examples: The parsimonious landlord refused to fix the heating.
A parsimonious budget left little room for new programs.

words.definition: unwilling to spend money; stingy
words.nuance: Also describes an amount that is insultingly small.
examples: The miserly old man counted every coin twice.
Workers called the company's raise miserly.

words.definition: extremely poor; also, extremely stingy
words.nuance: Can mean either poverty-stricken or miserly, so read the context.
examples: The penurious student lived on rice and beans.
His penurious habits kept him from enjoying his wealth.

words.definition: lasting for a very short time
words.nuance: Often used with a sense of fragile beauty or passing fashion.
examples: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.
The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms draws crowds every spring.

words.definition: lasting only a short time; impermanent
words.nuance: Also used as a noun for a person who is only passing through a place.
examples: The medication caused only transient side effects.
A transient population makes it hard to build community.

words.definition: soon passing out of sight, memory, or existence; vanishing
words.nuance: Emphasizes fading away gradually, like mist.
examples: The evanescent glow of the sunset faded within minutes.
Her evanescent smile disappeared as soon as the cameras left.

words.definition: hostile and aggressive; eager to fight
words.nuance: Also refers to a nation or party engaged in a war.
examples: The belligerent customer shouted at the cashier.
Each belligerent nation blamed the other for the war.

words.definition: demonstrating aggression and willingness to fight
words.nuance: Often describes rhetoric or policy that leans toward war.
examples: The minister's bellicose speech alarmed neighboring countries.
His bellicose tone ended any hope of compromise.

words.definition: eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight
words.nuance: Usually describes temperament: a pugnacious debater relishes a fight.
examples: The pugnacious senator relished a good argument.
A pugnacious little terrier barked at every passerby.

words.definition: excessively eager to please or obey
words.nuance: Implies fawning attentiveness, usually toward someone powerful.
examples: The obsequious waiter refilled our glasses every two minutes.
Staff grew obsequious whenever the CEO visited.

words.definition: behaving in a flattering way toward someone important to gain advantage
words.nuance: Stresses self-serving flattery.
examples: The film mocks the sycophantic aides who surround the dictator.
The sycophantic reviews made the critic seem bought.

words.definition: displaying exaggerated flattery or affection
words.nuance: Suggests an eager, almost groveling display.
examples: The star ignored the fawning crowd of reporters.
His fawning praise of the boss embarrassed everyone.

words.definition: to soothe the anger or anxiety of
words.nuance: Usually applied to a person whose feelings need calming.
examples: The manager offered a refund to mollify the angry customer.
Nothing she said could mollify her worried parents.

words.definition: to make someone less angry or hostile
words.nuance: Often implies concessions made to calm someone down.
examples: The company tried to placate investors with a new strategy.
He bought flowers to placate his irritated roommate.

words.definition: to make an unpleasant feeling less intense
words.nuance: Used for feelings and needs: assuage guilt, fear, hunger, or thirst.
examples: A sincere apology did little to assuage her guilt.
The report was meant to assuage fears about the bridge's safety.

words.definition: recklessly extravagant or wasteful in the use of resources
words.nuance: Can also mean morally dissolute.
examples: The profligate heir spent his fortune in a decade.
Critics attacked the government's profligate spending.

words.definition: spending money or resources freely and recklessly
words.nuance: Known from the parable of the prodigal son, who squanders his inheritance.
examples: The prodigal son returned home after wasting his inheritance.
Their prodigal use of water drained the reservoir.

words.definition: spending much more than is necessary or wise; exceeding reasonable limits
words.nuance: Also used for claims or behavior that go beyond what is reasonable.
examples: They threw an extravagant party with fireworks and a live orchestra.
Her extravagant claims were not supported by the data.
